subject: elephant
pitch: A gentle African elephant calf. Wrinkly slate-grey skin with a dusty, reddish tint from rolling in the dirt, huge fan-shaped ears with a pink flush on the inside, a curious trunk curling forward, stubby baby tusks, long lashes over kind brown eyes, a little tufted tail and round, padded feet with pale toenails.
reasoning:
I'm planning out a TypeScript module for an African elephant calf model, sizing it around 1.1 m shoulder height and 1.4 m body length, with coordinates set up so +Y is up, +Z is forward, and feet rest at y=0.

Now I'm defining the skeleton: a root "hips" joint, a spine chain built from a catmull-rom path running from hips through mid-back to the chest and neck base, and wrapping the torso in a sweep that follows this spine chain for the body mesh.

For the barrel-like body shape I'm setting the sweep radius as a function of t, bulging wider near the middle for both horizontal and vertical radii to get that rounded elephant silhouette. Then I'm planning the head as a separate scaled sphere joint attached near the top of the neck, and starting on the trunk as a long curling catmull path extending down from the head.

Now I'm working out the trunk's curl and taper, having it narrow from thick at the root to thin at the tip, and deciding to treat it as a chain parented to the head using a neck-like role. For the ears, I'm figuring out the coordinate frame for an extruded fan shape positioned at the sides of the head, working out which directions correspond to forward, up, and thickness so the ear outline sits correctly in the plane spanning height and depth.

I'm defining the fan-shaped outline points for the ear, then reasoning through which plane the ear should actually flare in — settling on the plane perpendicular to the head's x-axis so the broad ear face points sideways like a real elephant ear. Now I'm thinking about how to give it a grey outer face and pink inner face, considering either a second smaller extrude layer or a paint call based on face orientation.

Working out the paint logic: for each ear I need to flip which normal direction counts as "inner" depending on whether it's the left or right ear, so I define a side variable (+1 or -1) and check the sign of the normal's x-component times side to decide pink versus slate. Setting ear thickness to 0.025 with a small bevel, and now positioning the ear so it hangs from the upper side of the head at the correct attachment point.

To avoid confusion between local head-space axes and world coordinates, I'm deciding to just use absolute model-space coordinates for every placement and explicitly specify the bone (head) rather than relying on nearest-joint inference.

For the eyes, I'm placing dark brown spheres on the front sides of the head, roughly symmetric at x=±0.13, with lashes built as a ring of thin spikes around each eye using the ring helper with a defined angular range and tilt.

For the legs, I'm planning four pillar-like limbs with shoulders/hips positioned around the body and feet near ground level, using two-segment limbs with lengths around 0.45 each so the total reach slightly exceeds the vertical drop, and bending the front legs' elbows backward to match an elephant's natural stance.

For feet, I'm shaping squashed cylinders as padded bases with small pale toenail cylinders aimed forward and positioned along the front edge of each foot. I'm also setting up named joint chains (shoulder, elbow, wrist) for each limb so the bones can be referenced properly.

Now I'm working out parenting for the leg chains—hind legs attach to the hip joint while front legs attach to the top of the spine chain—and deciding how many joints the spine chain itself produces based on its path points.

For the neck, I'm planning a chain from the chest to the head using a short path of three points, with the final joint named "head" so it's distinct from the two neck joints before it, and it inherits orientation along the path direction.

For the body structure, I'm placing the hips as the root joint toward the back and running a catmull spine curve forward to the chest, then adding a tail chain of three joints curving down and back from the hips with a tapering sweep radius, finishing in a small tuft shape at the tip.

For skin material, I'm deciding between mottle and scales texture patterns, leaning toward scales with outlined cells since it naturally reads as wrinkly skin, blending slate and dusty-brown tones for the overall coloring.

Then I'm settling on a color palette - slate grays, dusty reds, ivory tusks, dark brown eyes - and planning the body coat as a mottled slate-to-brown pattern. For the tusks, I'm sketching curved cone sweeps emerging from the mouth corners using bezier curves that taper from thick at the base to a fine point, anchored to the head bone with ivory coloring.

For the mouth, I'm adding a jaw joint parented to the head with a small lower jaw part, keeping it simple since it's a minor feature. The trunk gets its own curved path from the head down toward the ground with a gentle curl at the tip, built as a chain of joints with a sweep that tapers from thick at the base to narrow at the end, colored to match the body coat.

I'm placing the head as a slightly stretched sphere, then positioning the ears at the sides using an attach point just outside the head's radius, oriented so they flare backward and outward like real elephant ears, with the thickness direction computed via cross product and the inner face getting a pink tint.

Working out the ear's fan-shaped outline...

I'm defining the paint function for pink inner-ear coloring based on normal direction and side, then setting up rigid attachment to the head bone. For the eyes, I'm figuring out placement on the head sphere's surface, using small embedded spheres positioned symmetrically at roughly x=±0.14, y=1.24, z=0.79, accounting for the ellipsoid's front curvature.

Now I'm adding lashes as a ring of small spikes around each eye, angled outward and tilted forward along the eye's facing direction, then mirroring the whole eye setup for both sides with a loop over s=[1,-1]. Next I'm moving on to the feet, sketching out pad geometry using a tapered cylinder shape at the foot joint.

Still working out foot and toenail placement...

Now I'm checking leg reachability — front and hind limb roots sit at y=0.92 with targets at y=0.06, giving a vertical span of 0.86, so I'm adjusting segment lengths to 0.46/0.44 to ensure the IK chain can reach with a slight bend, bending front legs backward and hind legs forward. I'm also working out the joint naming convention for the hip-knee-foot chain so the three-point limb output maps correctly.

Then I'm setting up parenting for legs (attaching front legs to the chest spine joint, hind legs to the hips) and assigning them a "leg" role, followed by building the neck chain with three control points producing neck1, neck2, and a tip joint named "head" for attaching the skull sphere oriented along the path's end tangent.

Next I work through the jaw joint under the head, tusk sweeps using bezier paths with pointed caps, and a small sphere nub at the trunk tip, positioning them relative to head and trunk joints. I sketch out the trunk sweep using the chain as its source with a tapering radius function, and the overall body sweep along the spine chain with varying radii to shape the rump, chest, and belly.

I spend a long stretch recalculating proportions for a calf-sized elephant -- lowering the body center, adjusting leg root positions and lengths, repositioning the neck and head centers, and working out where the trunk should emerge from the head and curl down toward the ground. I compute surface positions for the eyes and tusks using the head's ellipsoid equation to make sure they sit flush against the skull, then work through the ear geometry in detail: determining the outline's attachment point, how the local axes map to world z/x so the ears flare outward and backward correctly, and deriving the sign condition for painting the inner pink surface based on the ear's tilt and which side (left or right) it's on.

After that I settle on color treatments -- a mottled slate coat, a scaled wrinkle paint built from a palette of grayish tones for the body and head, plus separate colors for eyes, lashes, toenails, pink ear interior, tusks, and foot pads. Finally I start designing the tail: a tapering sweep for the tail itself, a tuft sphere at the tip, and a ring of small spike shapes arranged around the tip joint to suggest tail hairs, before moving into defining the tail chain itself.

Writing tail and spine chain definitions...

Now I'm fleshing out the body: defining the coat paint by layering countershading over mottled scale patterns, then building the hips, spine, neck, and head joints with a sweep for the body silhouette. I'm adding the jaw, tusks as tapered ivory sweeps, eyes with lash rings, pink-lined ear extrusions, a curling trunk with a tip nub, and a tufted tail, then setting up the leg chains using the limb helper for front and hind legs with named shoulder/elbow/foot and hip/knee/foot joints, checking that the reach distances stay within the limb segment lengths.

I'm now adding foot cylinders and small nail details positioned around the front edge of each foot, matching the orientation for hind feet too, then adding visible leg sweeps tapering from the body down to the ankles with flat end caps so they sit flush inside the foot cylinders instead of poking through the ground. I'm also adding a small mouth detail under the jaw and double-checking that no part sinks too far below the ground plane, that the proportions make sense for a calf, and that all the imports and type signatures (chain, sweep, limb, paint helpers) line up correctly before finalizing the code.
